metadata.note: Track ai-. Every figure from staleness_evidence.py (seed 20261127, numpy only — PPMI + SVD embeddings written by hand, no gensim/torch/downloads). FIRST DESIGN PRODUCED A NULL AND IS RECORDED: queries drawn uniformly from topic C left stale recall at 98.5% vs 100% fresh, because the surviving old terms carried the query. Rather than rig the query distribution, the measurement was rewritten as a SWEEP over how much of the query uses new language — which produced the real finding: staleness is harmless until the query stops using old vocabulary, and the genuinely dangerous case is not a missing word but a MIGRATED one, which fails silently at high confidence. Synthetic corpus from a stated generative process; the reel says so. Zero new components.

beats.narration_text: Salaam. This is Jainil. You build a search index over your documents once. A year goes by. The documents keep arriving, the vocabulary moves — new words appear, and a few old words quietly change which conversation they belong to. Nobody rebuilds the index. Today: what that actually does to your results, and which half of it you will never notice.

send arms terracotta, running indicator spins
two output lines land

props.command: Our search index is a year old. Results still look fine and scores are still high. Is it actually fine?
output: The scores will not tell you.
They did not move when the language did.

beats.narration_text: A stale index fails quietly. It does not throw and it does not come back empty — it returns five confident results from the wrong neighbourhood, with a similarity score that looks exactly like a good day.

beats.narration_text: Here is the setup. An index gets built on one year of text. Then the language moves, in two ordinary ways: new terms appear that the index has never seen, and one existing term migrates — it used to belong to infrastructure, and now it belongs to data. The index itself does not change. Nothing ever tells it to.

show.event: the index stage springs up
arrow draws, the language-moved stage lands
arrow draws, the unchanged-index stage lands and fills terracotta
the terracotta note: nothing triggers a rebuild

stages.label: Index built
stages.sub: one year of text, embedded once

stages.label: The language moves
stages.sub: new words; one word changes sides

props.title: WHAT ACTUALLY CHANGES
props.caption: The corpus drifts on its own schedule. The index only moves when somebody moves it.

beats.narration_text: So measure it. When none of the query uses new language, the stale index is perfect — a hundred percent recall, identical to a freshly rebuilt one. Half new words, still perfect, because the old words that survived carry the query on their own. It is only when the whole query is today's vocabulary that it breaks. And it breaks completely: zero percent.

show.event: legend sets: rebuilt in ink, stale in terracotta
the first two rows land, both pairs equal at 100
the all-new row lands and the stale bar is absent
the moved-word row lands, stale absent again

props.title: RECALL@5, BY HOW MUCH OF THE QUERY IS NEW LANGUAGE
props.caption: Stale is harmless right up until the query stops using the old vocabulary.

beats.narration_text: Which is two completely different failures wearing the same label. A word the index never learned fails loudly — there is no vector, so there is no result, and anybody watching sees an empty page. But a word that moved fails quietly. The index has a vector for pipeline. It is confident about it. It is simply pointing at where that word used to live. Recall, zero. Similarity on the top result, zero point eight nine. Every single result from the wrong topic.

show.event: two cards land left to right
the never-learned card fills — no vector, no result
the moved-word card lands in terracotta
caption lands under both

props.title: TWO FAILURES, ONE LABEL

cards.title: A word that moved
lines: It has a vector, and it is confident.
100% of results from the wrong topic.

props.caption: Recall is zero in both. Only one of them looks like it.

beats.narration_text: So the fix is not a bigger model. It is a clock and a canary. Re-embed on a cadence, because text drifts whether or not anybody is watching it. And monitor the out-of-vocabulary rate on live queries, because that is the one number that actually moves when the language moves. The similarity score will not tell you. Across these queries it fell by seven hundredths — from zero point nine six to zero point eight nine — while recall went from everything to nothing.

the terracotta note: this one never moved

stages.label: Re-embed on a clock
stages.sub: drift does not wait for a ticket

stages.label: Watch the OOV rate
stages.sub: it moves when the language moves

props.title: WHAT TO ACTUALLY MONITOR
props.caption: Not a bigger model. A clock, and a number that reacts.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Paste this into Claude. Take the last month of real queries against your search or your RAG system, and work out what fraction of their terms did not exist in the corpus the index was built on. Then go looking for the words that did exist but have changed what they sit next to. The first number tells you when to rebuild. The second tells you what you have been confidently getting wrong.
